rail_guard.text: Derry~Londonderry Station, on the far bank of the Foyle, which is the prettiest place to arrive in Ireland. I'm biased, but the view helps.
Hop aboard. The Wildlore rail runs to any town you have visited on this island. Where to?

wall_guide.text: Welcome to the Derry~Londonderry Walls! They're 1.5 kilometres round, up to 10 metres thick in places, and the only complete city walls left in Ireland.
Please stay on the walkway. The walls have stood for 400 years, but they've never had to deal with tourists with selfie sticks.

then.text: Roaring Meg liked you, then. She doesn't like everybody. She's a cannon. She has views.
Off along the top of the north wall, to the east end, and say hello to Meg's keeper. It's a fair stroll. Mind the pigeons, they have right of way.

else.text: Tell you what. Would you walk the north wall to the far end for me? Meg's keeper is out there with the old cannon, and she's had no visitors since the coach party.
These walls are over four hundred years old and nobody has ever got through them. Well, nobody except tourists. And pigeons.

then.text: Wet out, is it? Come in, the Tower Museum's lovely and dry. The stairs are free.
Sun's out! Walk the Walls today, you'll see right across the whole city.

museum_curator.text: The Tower Museum tells Derry~Londonderry's story in four floors and one very steep staircase. We say the climb is an exhibit in itself.
Doire means 'oak grove'. The city was named for a wood. Quite a few of the oaks are still around, and the rest are doing very well as furniture.

then.text: The Peace Bridge is floating in the fog today. Like it's dancing on a cloud.
Wind on the Foyle! The bridge isn't dancing today, it's doing a jig.
Dusk is the best crossing. The river goes all gold and pink, like a sweetie wrapper.

bridge_cyclist.text: {greeting} I cross the Peace Bridge four times a day. I don't need to. It's just that every time, the light on the river is different.
The bridge is built so it feels like it's dancing. You'll see. Take your time, even if you're late.

then.text: Rain on the Diamond. The acoustics stay great, it's the audience that runs away.
Late one? This is when the good tunes come out, slow and soft.

diamond_busker.text: {greeting} I play on the Diamond. Wonderful acoustics: four streets, four directions of shouting, and a statue at the middle to absorb the heckles.
Derry~Londonderry's known for its music, you know. Songs, fiddles, and a good melody in the kitchen at two in the morning.

then.text: Fog on the Foyle. The river's still there, it's just being mysterious.
First light on the water. The Foyle's at its calmest now, before anybody's had their tea.

ferry_pilot.text: The Foyle's a lovely river. Wide, easy, full of light. The sort of river that makes you want to write down what you're feeling. Then you remember you have a bus to catch.
The name Foyle comes from the Irish 'Feabhal', and it means 'lip' or 'edge'. The river sits on the edge of everything, like a politely lingering guest.

then.text: Meg's been quiet for a good while now, and I like her that way. A cannon with nothing to prove is the best sort.
You walked the whole way? Brilliant. Nobody walks it any more. They take photographs of it from the car park.
This is Roaring Meg. Cast in 1642. She's a quiet pensioner now, and she's polite to everyone who walks past her. Here, a bit of soda farl for the walk back.

else.text: Meg's a cannon from the 1600s. She's seen a lot and she's said nothing. If you fancy a walk, the guide at the other end will tell you about it.

derry_lamplighter.text: I light the old lamps along the Walls. Four hundred years of stone, and it still likes a bit of glow.
The Walls were never broken through, you know. They call it the Maiden City for that.
Quiet night. Just me, the lamps, and the odd cat on patrol.

derry_fox_watcher.text: Shh. There's a vixen comes down by the river most nights. Red torch only, it doesn't bother her.
Foxes in the city are cheeky wee things. One stole my sandwich last week. Fair play to her.
If you see two eyes glowing by the bins, say hello nicely. Don't follow, though.

der_shopper.text: Derry~Londonderry on a Saturday, you can't move for people and I wouldn't have it any other way.

then.text: It's only soft rain. If you flinch at that here, you'll be flinching for the rest of your life.

else.text: I came in for one loaf and I've three bags. That's the high street for you.

der_walker.text: I've done the whole circuit of the walls. Mile and a bit, cannons and all, and the views are class.
Best city walls in Ireland and they're all still standing. Take that, every other siege.

der_visitor.text: The guide said the murals tell the whole story of Derry~Londonderry. I've been looking at them for an hour and I'm still welling up.

then.text: Sun on the old stone and a cup of tea. I might never go home.

else.text: Everyone here says hello. Even the dogs. I'm not used to it, and I love it.

der_jogger.text: Round the green, up the steps, down the hill. By the time I'm home I've earned a bun. A big one.
Don't let the friendly faces fool you, this city is steeper than it looks.

then.text: Áine says the cake was gone by teatime. Come back for a farl any time. Pounds or euros. Not both at once.
You're back! She liked it? She liked it. Oh, a card. I'm not crying. It's the flour.
That's the open border for you. A cake goes out of the UK, into the EU, and nobody asks it for its passport.
Áine's in Donegal Town, out the west road past Glenveagh, then south. You'll be in the Republic before the icing sets.

else.text: {greeting} Are you headed west? It's my sister Áine's birthday, her cake needs taking to Donegal Town, and my van's dead.
Over the border, mind. Don't worry, there isn't one. Well, there is. You just can't see it.
Take Áine's birthday cake to Donegal Town?

then.text: You're a star. West road out of town, through Glenveagh, then south to Donegal Town. Say hello to the walker on the border road, he knows everyone.

else.text: No bother. It's a lemon drizzle, it'll keep. Áine won't.
